Ross2011.content:
- **Study/species and sample:** *Macaca mulatta* in vivo strain experiments: **4 animals** (3 adult females, 1 adult male), with right-side enucleation performed years earlier. Additional in vivo comparison: one *Chlorocebus aethiops* experiment (experiment 57). The FE geometry was a museum *Macaca fascicularis* skull.
- **Loading and measurement:** In vivo animals incised and chewed foods; chewing side was recorded. Strain gauges (rectangular rosettes or stacked delta rosettes) measured bone strain at facial sites. No DIC was reported. The FE model simulated unilateral postcanine biting with eight muscle loads: superficial and deep masseter, medial pterygoid, and anterior temporalis, bilaterally. Six bite constraints were tested: left M³, M², M¹, P⁴, P³, or all left postcanine teeth.
- **FE construction/materials/solver:** Built from **61 CT scans, 2 mm thick**; mesh of **311,047 brick and tetrahedral elements**. Material properties were based on macaque-skull data (Wang & Dechow, 2006); **numerical material-property values are not given in this text**. Solver: **Strand 7.4**. Muscle-force ratios used EMG and physiological cross-sectional-area data.
- **Boundary conditions:** Working-side articular-eminence node fixed against Y/Z translation; balancing-side eminence node fixed against X/Y/Z translation. Bite-point tooth cusp(s) constrained against X/Y/Z translation. Same muscle forces and TMJ constraints across the six bite-point solutions.
- **Agreement and quantitative findings:** No slope, R², percentage error, or overall microstrain error metric is reported. Orientation agreement was assessed by overlap of FE and in vivo orientation ranges: e.g., postorbital bar working **3/5**, balancing **1/4**; anterior zygomatic root **1/2** working and **2/2** balancing; middle zygomatic arch **0/3** on either side (Table 5). Magnitude comparison covered **20 sites**: raw FE strains were below in vivo ranges at **6 sites**. Normalizing by anterior-arch strain brought most FE values within in vivo ranges, except left septum, right postorbital bar, and right dorsal orbital sites. Simultaneous in vivo shear-strain means included working-side arch **389 με**, corpus **318 με**, bar **69 με**; balancing-side arch **390 με**, corpus **400 με**, bar **343 με**.
- **Error sources/recommendations:** Authors cite differences in skull size/stiffness, individuals/species, material properties, muscle estimates, gauge placement/orientation, and unrecorded bite location and food properties. Recommended practices include realistic muscle forces, material properties and constraints; validation against experimental strain data; carefully documenting gauge placement; and using multiple subjects. **No accuracy target is specified.**
- **Tongue-pressure/remodeling information:** No tongue-pressure measurements, tongue forces, palatal strains, sutural outcomes, or bone-remodeling results are reported.
- **Full text visible:** Yes—the supplied page content includes the article text, methods, results, and conclusions.

ToroIbacache2016.content:
- **Full text visibility:** Yes—the supplied page includes the article’s full text. It does **not** report the planned pig-maxilla study, comparisons among FEBio/CalculiX/JAX, or tongue-pressure modeling results.
- **Species and sample:** Human, not pig. Bone properties came from two fresh-frozen human cadavers (female, age 22; male, age 42). In-vitro strain validation used the male specimen; three loading trials are reported.
- **Loading and measurement:** Simulated left third-premolar (P³) biting. The applied in-vitro load magnitude is not stated in the visible text. Strain was measured at 14 craniofacial locations using strain gauges, then compared with a specimen-specific FE model. DIC is not reported.
- **Materials:** Human cortical-bone Young’s modulus was spatially heterogeneous: 17.92–25.52 GPa (mean 20.61 GPa, SD 1.92); Poisson’s ratio 0.293. Trabecular bone: 637 MPa, Poisson’s ratio 0.28. Enamel: 80,000 MPa, Poisson’s ratio 0.28.
- **Solver and conditions:** Strand7 FEA software. The in-vitro model replicated the experimental loading; specific validation-model boundary-condition details are not given in the visible text. In the main feeding simulations, the working-side TMJ node was fixed in all translation axes; the balancing-side TMJ was constrained superoinferiorly and anteroposteriorly; the tooth-bite node was constrained superoinferiorly.
- **Agreement:** Regressions on log-transformed strain: maximum principal strain, slope 0.845, intercept 0.194, R² = 0.909, p < 0.001; minimum principal strain, slope 0.849, intercept 0.186, R² = 0.953, p < 0.001. Table 6 reports percentage errors from 0.79% to 80%. Example: site 3 maximum-principal-strain error was 80%, but the absolute difference was only 2.67 με. Site 10 maximum-principal-strain error was 49.26%. Strain orientations at all 14 sites were described as very similar.
- **Sources of error and practices:** High percentage errors could arise at low-strain sites. The authors identify potential modeling error from the thin anterior maxillary-sinus wall and simplifications of thin nasal-cavity bones. They recommend/illustrate specimen-specific validation against in-vitro strain magnitudes and orientations across multiple sites; they note that earlier tooth-point-loading validation omitted muscle loading. No explicit accuracy threshold is recommended; reported validation R² values exceeded 0.9.
- **Tongue pressures, forces, strains, or sutural/bone outcomes:** Absent from this page.

BrightRayfield2011.content:
- **Species/sample:** Domestic pig (*Sus scrofa*), one Large White specimen, approximately 6 months old; skull 247 × 141 × 133 mm. The experiment was repeated three times per gauge group.
- **Loading:** Ex vivo static, idealized muscle loading—not palatal pressure. Experimental targets: right masseter 300 N, left temporalis 200 N, left masseter 200 N, right temporalis 100 N. Mean corrected loads applied in FE: 282, 195, 178 and 100 N, respectively (total 755 N).
- **Measurement:** Sixteen planar three-grid rosette strain gauges; G1 was excluded for drift and G6 for poor repeatability, leaving 14 reliable gauges. No DIC was used.
- **Materials:** Initial homogeneous isotropic model: E = 12.5 GPa, Poisson’s ratio ν = 0.35, including teeth. Heterogeneous variants used a one-element-thick (0.92 mm) cortical shell with those properties and cancellous interior E = 6 or 1 GPa; interior ν = 0.35 or 0.2.
- **FE setup:** Abaqus 6.8.2. Main model: 1,749,149 quadratic 10-node tetrahedra. Constraints fixed translation in x, y and z at 25 nodes bilaterally at each TMJ, and in the dorsoventral y direction at 20 nodes bilaterally at the first molars.
- **Agreement/results:** The article reports no slope, R² or overall percentage validation error. Models were approximately an order of magnitude too stiff; principal strain magnitudes and some strain ratios were not reproduced correctly. Principal-strain orientations were mostly within 10° of experiment; G8, G11, G14 and G16 differed by 25–40°. Experimental maximum principal strain ranged from −8.4 με at G6 to 485 με at G7; minimum principal strain ranged from −606 με at G8 to −6 με at G1. Examples: G5 measured 456 με tension and −288 με compression; G8 measured 68 and −606 με.
- **Error drivers/recommendations:** Material-property assumptions and unresolved local bone heterogeneity/structure were implicated; CT resolution and missing pig-bone material data limited modeling. Gauge placement/strain gradients particularly affected G5. Loading changes and membrane elements generally had small effects. Use converged meshes and consistent assumptions for comparative models; exercise caution with absolute strain, breaking-stress and bite-force predictions. Mesh convergence was within 5% at gauge sites, except G7 (12%); this is not a validation-accuracy target.
- **Requested information absent:** No FEBio/CalculiX/JAX comparison, palatal-pressure test, or tongue-pressure/force, remodeling, or sutural outcome data. Full article text was visible in the supplied page content.

Panagiotopoulou2017.content:
- **Species / sample:** One adult female rhesus macaque (*Macaca mulatta*), chewing grapes. No pig maxilla, palatal-pressure loading, tongue-pressure study, or cross-solver comparison is reported.
- **Loading:** Subject-specific jaw-elevator muscle forces estimated from normalized EMG amplitude × physiological cross-sectional area (PCSA) × specific muscle tension (30 N/cm²). Forces were applied at either maximum total muscle activation or the time of maximum strain in the lower lateral gauge (LLAT). The study did not apply a specified pressure load.
- **Measurements:** Three delta-rosette strain gauges on the left mandibular corpus: medial/lingual (MED), lower lateral/buccal (LLAT), and upper lateral/buccal (ULAT). Strain and EMG were sampled at 5 kHz; reported in-vivo statistics represent 163 chews per gauge. No DIC was used.
- **Materials:** Cortical bone had 80 heterogeneous, orthotropic material-property assignments derived from the same animal’s CT density and ex-vivo cortical-bone measurements. Trabecular tissue and teeth were isotropic, homogeneous, with Poisson’s ratio 0.3; trabecular Young’s modulus tested at 1, 2, 3, or 10 GPa; teeth at 17 or 24.5 GPa. PDL: 0.00068 GPa, ν=0.49. Titanium screws: 105 GPa, ν=0.36.
- **Solver / model:** Abaqus 6.13, implicit direct static solver; approximately 10 minutes per model using 4 processors and 8 tokens.
- **Boundary conditions:** Tie constraints bonded intersecting surfaces. Sensitivity tests varied which TMJ was fixed and which axes were constrained, plus bite-tooth constraints. Best overall agreement was Model H: left TMJ and left premolars and first molar constrained in all translations; right TMJ constrained in X and Y; muscle forces set at peak LLAT strain.
- **Agreement:** No regression slope, R², percentage error, or aggregate accuracy target is reported. In-vivo mean ε₁/ε₂ (με): ULAT 81/−90; LLAT 56/−48; MED 50/−69. Model H: ULAT 127/−98; LLAT 80/−70; MED 32/−41. H was closer than Model G at ULAT and LLAT; G was closer at MED. Model strains were generally higher than in vivo.
- **Error drivers / recommendations:** TMJ and bite-point constraints had the strongest effects; force-estimation timing also altered strain magnitudes and orientations. Tooth material changes had negligible effects. The authors recommend subject-specific geometry/material data, sensitivity analyses, careful specification of TMJ and bite constraints, and documenting force timing through the chewing cycle. They identify 10 GPa isotropic, homogeneous trabecular tissue as suitable in this model; no numerical accuracy target is given.
- **Full text:** Visible in the supplied page content. The requested pig-pressure, tongue-pressure/force, sutural-outcome, and FEBio/CalculiX/JAX results are absent.

Liu2008JOMS.content:
- **Full text visibility:** Yes; the supplied page includes the article’s full text.
- **Study/model:** Twelve 12-week-old Yucatan miniature pigs, arranged as six sibling pairs. One pig per pair underwent tongue-volume reduction; the other received sham incisions. Reduction was reported as **23–25%** in the abstract and **20–25%** in the methods.
- **Loading and measurements:** Unrestrained natural mastication of pig chow. Bone strains were measured using rosette strain gauges at the palatal premaxilla (PM) and lingual mandibular incisor (MI) and molar (MM) alveolar sites, plus single-element gauges across the palatal premaxillary suture (PMS) and lingual mandibular symphysis (MSP). Pressure transducers measured the maxillary palatal site (PAL) and mandibular lingual site (MAN). No DIC or direct force measurement was reported. Resting values were not measured; only dynamic chewing-cycle changes were analyzed.
- **Pig results:** Pressures ranged **2.12–8.04 kPa**; MAN pressure exceeded PAL pressure on both sides (**p < 0.05**). Tongue reduction lowered pressures (**p < 0.01**); the article reports decreases of **50% or more** at PAL and MAN in the abstract/results, and, in the discussion, approximately **35–40% at PAL** versus **65–70% at MAN**. Rosette-site principal strains were **below 100 με in most measures**. PM strain was compression-dominant; MI and MM were tension-dominant. MM tensile strain exceeded PM (**p < 0.05**). PMS strain was tensile, with a largest value of about **200 με**; MSP strain was compressive. Reduction decreased strain magnitudes overall by **18–48%**, significantly at MI on the balancing side; PMS tensile strain decreased significantly on the working side, while MSP strain showed no change. At PM and MI, tensile orientation shifted from latero-anterior to latero-posterior (**p < 0.05–0.001**); MM changed little.
- **Other pressure figures cited in the article:** Human tongue pressures during mastication on the hard palate ranged **0.8–17.1 kPa**. Cited human tooth pressures: resting **0–2 g/cm²** (negative at specified teeth), chewing **50–150 g/cm²**, swallowing **200–350 g/cm²**.
- **FE-validation details requested:** No material assignments or values, FE solver, boundary conditions, agreement metric, slope, R², percentage error, or FE-versus-measurement microstrain results are reported. No error drivers or accuracy targets are given. The article is not a CT-based FE guidance paper and gives no concrete validation-practice recommendations.

Liu2008AOB.content:
- **Species:** Yucatan miniature pigs.
- **Sample:** Five sibling pairs (10 animals), 12 weeks old; three male pairs and two female pairs. One animal in each pair received tongue-volume reduction; its sibling received sham surgery.
- **Loading/intervention:** No applied palatal pressure. The anterior two-thirds of the tongue was reduced by conical-wedge glossectomy, targeting about 15% reduction. Postmortem tongue volume and weight losses were **15.21 ± 0.78%** and **15.18 ± 0.19%**, respectively. The abstract reports reduction of **15–17%**.
- **Measurements:** Serial lateral and axial cephalograms at baseline and 2 and 4 weeks after surgery; skull osteometry after euthanasia; DEXA measurements of bone mineral density (BMD) and content (BMC). Tongue dimensions were measured using longitudinal tongue impressions/casts. **No strain gauges, DIC, or strain measurements** are reported.
- **Material assignment/values, FE solver, boundary conditions, agreement metric, and quantitative FE validation results:** **Not reported**; this is not an FE study. No slope, R², percentage error, or microstrain results are provided.
- **Error drivers or validation recommendations/accuracy targets:** No FE error analysis or quantitative accuracy targets are given. The authors recommend **long-term growth tracking** for young subjects undergoing tongue-volume reduction, either alone for true macroglossia or adjunctively with other orthopaedic procedures.
- **Tongue pressure/force and skeletal outcomes:** The study reports no measured tongue pressure or force values. It cites a separate prior loading study, stating that tongue loads decreased on anterior mandibular symphysis and premaxilla after volume reduction, while posterior mandibular corpus and maxillary palate loads were less affected; numerical loads are not supplied. No strains or sutural outcomes are reported. In this study, craniofacial growth was slower in reduction animals: premaxillary palatal length and mandibular symphysis length were significantly smaller at 2 and 4 weeks; anterior mandibular length, ramus height, maxillary palatal length, midfacial width, anterior mandibular width, and canine-level mandibular arch width were smaller at skull measurement. BMD and BMC across bone blocks were **4.8–16.5% lower** in reduction animals; mandibular symphysis BMC was significantly lower.
- **Full text visible:** Yes—the supplied page content includes the article text and tables.

Deng2018.content:
- **Full text:** Yes—the supplied page includes the article’s full text and tables.
- **Species and sample:** 22 Yucatan minipigs, aged 12 weeks, arranged as 11 same-gender sibling pairs. One animal per pair received tongue reduction and the other sham surgery. Acute measurements: 6 pairs (3 male, 3 female), immediately after surgery. Chronic measurements: 5 pairs (3 male, 2 female), 1 month after surgery.
- **Loading and measurement:** Under 3–5% isoflurane anesthesia, bilateral hypoglossal nerve trunk (HG), medial branch (HGM), lateral branch (HGL), genioglossus (GG), and styloglossus (SG) were electrically stimulated. Stimuli: 600-ms trains; nerves, 0.5-ms pulses at 3–15 V; muscles, 5-ms pulses at 10–40 V. Typical tetanic intensities were 6–9 V for nerves and 20–30 V for muscles. Bone strain and pressure signals were recorded. Three rosette gauges measured strains at premaxilla (PM), mandibular incisor (MI), and mandibular molar (MM); single-element gauges measured premaxillary-maxillary suture (PMS) and mandibular symphysis (MSP); pressure transducers measured palatal process (PAL) and mandibular corpus (MAN). No DIC was reported.
- **FE/modeling details:** Material assignment/values, FE solver, boundary conditions, agreement metrics, validation slope or R², percentage error, error drivers, and FE accuracy targets are **not reported**. No solver comparison or CT-based FE validation is described.
- **Tongue-related outcomes:** Discussion reports bone pressures of **1.0–10 kPa** during stimulation and mastication; site-specific pressure values and tongue forces are not provided in the supplied text. Acute reduction significantly decreased PAL pressure under HG, HGM, and HGL stimulation; MAN pressure did not show this decrease. Chronic PAL differences diminished; MAN pressure decreased, particularly under HG. Principal tensile and compressive strains were generally reported as **<100 με**, although tabled values include larger results—for example, acute MM under HG in reduction animals: tensile **95.2 με**, compressive **−60.2 με**, shear **155.4 με**. Acute sham versus reduction PM shear under HG was **26.9 versus 15.3 με**. Chronic comparisons reported reduced PM shear by **29–77%** in 3 of 4 comparisons and reduced MI shear by **32–58%** in 4 of 5. Acute reduction enhanced posterior MM loading; this compensatory enhancement diminished with healing. PMS strain changed from consistently tensile in sham animals to mixed patterns acutely; MSP showed significantly larger compressive strain acutely. No quantitative sutural deformation values are supplied.
- **Recommendations:** The authors call for further study of long-term tongue-volume relapse and whether altered loading persists; no concrete modeling practices or accuracy targets are given.

Maas2012.content:
- **Full text visibility:** Yes. The supplied page contains the article’s full text.
- **Species, sample size, loading of an ex vivo maxilla/palate, strain-gauge/DIC measurements, material assignments and values, boundary conditions, and FEBio/CalculiX/JAX comparison:** **Absent.** The page does not describe that study.
- **Resting tongue pressures/forces, strains, and sutural or bone outcomes:** **Absent.** The page does not discuss tongue-pressure-driven maxillary remodeling.
- **Solver information available:** FEBio is a nonlinear implicit finite-element framework written in C++; it supports quasi-static and dynamic analyses, uses implicit time integration, and includes linear-solver support for PARDISO, SUPERLU, and WSMP. The article does not compare FEBio with CalculiX or JAX.
- **Verification and agreement results reported:** The FEBio Verification Suite contains **over 140 test problems**. Reported comparisons include:
  - Twisted-ribbon shell test: FEBio differed from the analytical solution by **less than 2%** using half of 2048 elements; with 32 elements, the difference was **approximately 30%**.
  - Crushing a pipe: peak forces from FEBio, NIKE3D, and ABAQUS differed by **less than 3%**.
  - Compressed cartilage layer: FEBio and NIKE3D stresses were nearly identical; ABAQUS stresses differed by **less than 3%**.
  - Other tests are described as showing excellent, nearly identical, or good agreement, without reported slope, R², percentage-error, or microstrain statistics.
- **Reported causes of differences:** Differences were attributed to numerical algorithms, including different contact-enforcement algorithms; differences in the Mooney–Rivlin dilatational strain-energy implementation; and differences in enforcement of material incompressibility.
- **Concrete recommendations:** The article states that **problem-specific verification, mesh-convergence studies, and validation are necessary** to establish accuracy for a specific problem. It emphasizes comparing numerical results with analytical solutions or results from established, verified FE codes. It gives no general accuracy target.

Henninger2010.content:
| Requested item | Information in the page |
|---|---|
| Study/model and species | The page is a review of verification and validation in computational biomechanics. It does not describe a CT-based ex vivo pig maxilla/palate study or a tongue-pressure remodeling study; species are not stated for those requested studies. |
| Sample size, loading, measurements | No sample size, 10–70 kPa palatal loading, or detailed gauge/DIC protocol is reported. A cited pelvic-bone example used direct mechanical testing to simulate body-weight loading through the hip joint and strain gauges to measure cortical-bone deformation; no sample size or loading values are given. |
| Material assignment/values, solver, boundary conditions | No pig maxilla/palate material assignments or values, FEBio/CalculiX/JAX comparison, or associated boundary conditions are reported. The review notes that biological-tissue models commonly used literature-derived mean material properties and examined their variance with sensitivity analysis. |
| Agreement metrics/results and error sources | No slope, R², percentage error, or microstrain results for the requested studies are reported. The review discusses percent change from nominal, root-mean-square error, correlation coefficients/R², and Bland–Altman analysis. It warns correlation measures association, not agreement, and can be artificially high when data variation exceeds measurement error. Error sources discussed include uncertain material properties, specimen variability and protocol differences, image-resolution/3D-geometry reconstruction, unrealistic in-vitro boundary conditions, discretization, incomplete iterative convergence, programming errors, and round-off. |
| Tongue-pressure evidence | No measured tongue pressures or forces, strains, or maxillary sutural/bone outcomes are reported. |

**Concrete recommendations and targets stated in the review**

- Verify before validation; address code verification and calculation/discretization verification separately. Test against exact analytical solutions where available, then semi-analytic and accurate numerical solutions.
- A cited constitutive-code test predicted stress within **3%** of an analytical solution; this verifies only that tested case, not other responses.
- Perform mesh convergence; spinal-segment studies cited **<5%** change in solution output as adequate. Report mesh quality as iterative percentage change, and report elements, nodes, and element types.
- Conduct sensitivity analysis before validation to identify critical parameters and help design controlled experiments; reassess after validation. Monte Carlo methods can assess parameter combinations.
- Plan validation by PIRT and progress through constituent benchmark problems, subsystems, then complete-system analysis. Report experimental means, standard deviations, and number of independent measurements.
- Report device accuracy as **mean ± 1.96 standard deviations**; include device tolerances and independently check accuracy.
- Use quantitative metrics and account for experimental uncertainty and numerical error; consider non-deterministic metrics incorporating input-parameter probability distributions.
- For method comparisons, consider Bland–Altman plots: plot **E−S** against **(E+S)/2**, and test the difference against zero.

**Full text visible:** Yes; the supplied page includes the full review text.

Anderson2007.content:
| Requested item | Information explicitly available in the page |
|---|---|
| Species; sample size (*n*); loading; measurements; material assignments and values; FE solver; boundary conditions for the planned pig-maxilla study | **Not stated.** The page does not describe the proposed pig-maxilla study, its 10–70 kPa loading, strain gauges, or FEBio/CalculiX/JAX comparison. |
| Agreement results for the planned study | **Not stated.** No slope, *R*², percent error, or microstrain results for that study appear in the page. |
| Error drivers for the planned study | **Not stated.** The article discusses possible numerical errors (including discretization, iterative, round-off, coordinate-transformation, and symmetry errors) and modeling errors (including geometry, boundary conditions, material properties, and constitutive equations), but does not identify drivers in the proposed study. |
| Tongue pressure/force, strains, and sutural or bone outcomes | **Not stated.** The page contains no tongue-pressure or maxillary-remodeling study. |

**Guidance and concrete recommendations in the article**

- Establish the model’s **intended use** before planning verification and validation (V&V); select validation experiments and metrics to match the responses of interest.
- **Verify before validating.** Code verification tests implementation against known solutions; calculation verification estimates numerical error. Commercial software does not remove the analyst’s responsibility for further verification.
- For calculation verification, conduct mesh-convergence studies using the **intended validation parameter** as the primary convergence criterion. Mesh convergence indicates refinement is unlikely to change predictions significantly; it does **not** establish accuracy.
- For buckling models, first find a minimum mesh that captures converged buckling behavior, then compare refinements.
- Use benchmark problems, ranked by accuracy: exact analytical/manufactured solutions; semi-analytical solutions; highly accurate numerical solutions. Published numerical benchmarks should be documented and verified, include numerical-error estimates, and be independently reproduced.
- Design validation experiments collaboratively where possible, with consistent loading and boundary conditions. Prefer a hierarchical sequence: unit problems, benchmark cases, subsystem cases, complete systems. Report experimental random and systematic errors; use means and standard deviations.
- Choose quantitative validation metrics that account for experimental and computational uncertainty. The most comprehensive, non-deterministic approach uses experimentally estimated input distributions and reports computational results as **mean ± 2 standard deviations**.
- Perform sensitivity studies before testing to identify influential inputs and revisit them after validation. Avoid treating calibration as validation.

**Article’s numerical examples—not target accuracy standards:** constitutive-model predictions differed from analytical results by **less than 3%**; a refined ligament mesh’s average strains differed by **less than 1%** from a mesh with twice as many elements. A pelvis example reported *R*² = **0.776** and regression line **y = 0.933x − 0.298**. The article specifies **no universal accuracy target**; acceptable accuracy depends on intended use, engineering judgment, and peer review.

**Full text visible:** Yes—the supplied page includes the article’s full text.

**Concrete recommended practices:** Report model name, version, intended use, limitations, anatomical source and imaging modality/resolution, segmentation method and errors, coordinate system and zero-load reference state, and subcomponent geometry. Describe each load or constraint by type, application region, magnitude, direction, time history, and physiological rationale; identify primary and secondary outputs. Report material formulation, all coefficients, their sources and fitting procedures, other required properties, and component interactions and properties. Document element name, shape, formulation, acceptance criteria, node/element counts, and average edge length. Name the FE software and version; report solution strategy, numerical algorithms, convergence tolerances, defaults used, and post-processing. Report verification methods, implementation checks, comparisons with known solutions, sensitivity to solver settings, mesh-convergence outputs, and repeatability across platforms. For validation, identify the procedure, validated output and its relevance, assumptions, parameter justification, development and comparison data sources, input uncertainties, sensitivity-analysis parameters and perturbations, and predictive limitations. For multiscale work, report coupling approach, scale-separation justification, RVE adequacy/size effects, and mechanical consistency.

**Full text:** The article text was visible in the supplied page content. Appendix A is identified as supplementary material, but its contents are not included.

Henak2013.content:
- **Full text:** Yes—the supplied page includes the article’s abstract, methods, results, discussion, and conclusion. Some equations and figure content are not rendered in the supplied text.
- **Study and species:** Human cadaveric hip study, not pig maxilla or palate. **n = 5** normal male specimens; age **40 ± 14 years**, weight **62.8 ± 13.8 kg**, height **176.5 ± 8.9 cm**.
- **Loading:** Four physiological hip-loading scenarios: walking heel strike, walking mid-stance, stair-descent heel strike, and stair-ascent heel strike. Selected-trial resultant loads, respectively, were **1560 ± 335 N**, **1520 ± 327 N**, **1723 ± 326 N**, and **1464 ± 284 N**. No palatal pressures or tongue loads are reported.
- **Measurements:** Contact stress and area were measured with **Fuji Prescale pressure-sensitive film**, not strain gauges or DIC. Cartilage material behavior was measured by unconfined compression. No microstrain measurements are reported.
- **Material assignment and values:** Cortical bone was isotropic linear elastic: **E = 17 GPa, ν = 0.29**. Cartilage models were average neo-Hookean (“nH average”), average Veronda–Westmann (“VW average”), and specimen-/region-specific Veronda–Westmann (“VW specific”); near-incompressibility was enforced, but bulk-modulus values are not given. Pooled whole-joint coefficients: nH **μ = 5.32 ± 2.32 MPa**; VW **C₁ = 0.34 ± 0.24 MPa**, **C₂ = 6.55 ± 2.07** (unitless). The specific model used **25 coefficient sets each** for femur and acetabulum.
- **Solver and boundary conditions:** **NIKE3D**. Registration-block positions were aligned to digitized experimental positions; each model was run to the corresponding experimental load. Mesh convergence led to **five elements through cartilage thickness**.
- **Agreement and error:** Pixel-wise contact-stress RMS error: nH **23.8 ± 4.8%**, VW average **23.9 ± 4.8%**, VW specific **23.3 ± 4.8%**. Experimental peak stress was **13.8 ± 2.8 MPa**; VW-average FE peak was **16.4 ± 7.8 MPa**. ICC and clustered Bland–Altman analyses were performed, but numerical ICCs, slopes, and R² are not stated. No quantitative contact-area differences are provided.
- **Error and recommendations:** Pressure-sensitive film has stated **10–15%** contact-stress error; modeled film insertion changed peak stress by **<1%**. nH underpredicted peak stress in high-stress areas; VW average predicted peak stress, average stress, area, and patterns accurately. Specific coefficients did not improve predictions. The authors prefer average VW coefficients for normal cartilage; apply cautiously to degenerated cartilage. Neither the requested FEBio/CalculiX/JAX comparison nor tongue-pressure, maxillary-strain, or sutural/bone-outcome results appears in this page.

Erdemir2019.content:
| Requested item | Information explicitly available on this page |
|---|---|
| Species and sample size | No pig maxilla/palate study is described. The page concerns **human cadaver knees**: Open Knee(s), eight knees from eight donors; Natural Knee Data, seven knees from five donors. The project selected Open Knee(s) specimen oks003 and Natural Knee Data specimen DU02. |

Rafferty2019.content:
| Requested item | Information explicitly reported |
|---|---|
| Species / animals | Pig, *Sus scrofa*: domestic pigs; Hanford or Sinclair minipigs (normal-snouted); Yucatan minipigs; and Yucatan micropigs. |
| Sample sizes | External morphology: Hanford minipigs, n=11; Yucatan minipigs, n=11. CT: domestic pigs, n=3; normal minipigs, n=1; Yucatan minipigs, n=5; Yucatan micropigs, n=1. Decalcified histology: domestic pig, n=1; normal minipigs, n=4; Yucatan minipigs, n=4. Undecalcified gap measurements: domestic pig, n=1; Yucatans, n=3. Masticatory strain: normal minipigs, n=11; Yucatan minipigs, two 5-month-old females (four gauges across two pigs). Cyclic loading: domestic pigs, n=3; Yucatan minipigs, n=4. |
| Loading and measurements | In vivo mastication: single-element strain gauges placed perpendicular to nasofrontal and internasal sutures; recordings for 10–15 min after recovery from anesthesia. Cyclic tensile loading: posts surgically installed on right frontal and nasal bones; daily loading at 3.0 Hz for 30 min under anesthesia for 5 days. On the final day, gauges measured nasofrontal, coronal, interfrontal, and internasal strains. CT and histology assessed morphology; undecalcified sections measured suture-gap width. No DIC reported. |
| Quantitative results | Masticatory nasofrontal strain: normal −2012 με (SD 770, n=11; range −682 to −2892); Yucatan −909 με (SD 340, four gauges on two pigs; range −353 to −1265). Yucatan internasal readings: −110 με and +118 με (one each); normal post. internasal −440 με (SD 238, n=6; range −109 to −761). Nasofrontal gap: normal 238 μm; Yucatan mean 180 μm (SD 14, n=3, P<0.02). Coronal gap: normal 146 μm; Yucatan mean 72 μm (SD 9, n=2, P=0.055). Cyclic-loading strains (normal vs Yucatan, με): loaded nasofrontal +1689±489 vs +1992±432; opposite nasofrontal +1005±368 vs +1056±130; loaded coronal −836±464 vs −328±91; opposite coronal −283 to +113 vs −47 to +86; internasal −68 to +245 vs +453±127; interfrontal +270±236 vs −217 to +173. Breed differences were not significant. |
| FE / validation details | No FE model, solver, material assignment or values, boundary conditions for an FE model, agreement metric, slope, R², percent error, or accuracy target is reported. No 10–70 kPa palatal-pressure experiment is reported. |
| Interpretation / recommendations | Yucatan sutures were narrower and less interdigitated, with less organized ligament and more osteoblasts; they were not fused and responded mechanically to cyclic loading. Whether loading enhanced Yucatan sutural growth was not evaluated; clinical efficacy was not demonstrated. The authors envision less traumatic approaches, such as motorized reverse-pull headgear. No resting-tongue pressure/force, tongue-driven remodeling, or tongue-related strain outcomes are reported. |
